author: sharma_views
reason: Matches negative query criteria: Delhi domestic pollution discourse
text:
Two days of continuous rain in Delhi made me realise something about our pollution problem.

While it was raining, the air felt remarkably clean. I could breathe comfortably. But within a short time of the rain stopping, especially at night, I could feel the pollution returning with every breath. Even with trees and greenery around, that familiar heaviness in the air was back.

And this is why I find it difficult to accept the constant blame placed on farmers for Delhi's pollution.

Stubble burning certainly contributes. But I suspect its share is closer to 10–15%, while a much larger portion, perhaps 70–80%, comes from within Delhi-NCR itself.

What struck me was how quickly the pollution returned. Delhi itself has very little farmland, and I find it difficult to believe that distant farm fires alone explain such a rapid change in air quality. To me, this points towards a much bigger local pollution problem.

One thing I've noticed repeatedly is the amount of loose dust along our roads and footpaths. So many stretches have exposed soil and hardly any greenery. Every passing vehicle sends that dust into the air, where it mixes with exhaust fumes and other pollutants.

Rain settles this dust temporarily. Once the roads dry, the same cycle begins again.

We talk so much about vehicle emissions, but hardly anyone discusses the dust those very vehicles keep throwing back into the air.

I believe this is one area where Delhi could make a real difference. Cover the exposed soil, develop green strips along roads, maintain footpaths properly and stop leaving bare, dusty patches everywhere.

It sounds simple, but imagine the impact if this were done properly across Delhi-NCR. It wouldn't eliminate every source of pollution, but I strongly believe it could reduce a significant part of the problem.

🇮🇷|Pezeshkian Announces Step-by-Step Reform of Fuel Subsidies. The Voucher System Is the Mechanism. The Question Is Who Holds the Voucher.

President Masoud Pezeshkian stated: "We will resolve the issues step by step. We will gradually reform the gasoline and diesel issue and allocate its funds to the voucher system and people's livelihoods. If we save on water and electricity, we'll have a lot of money at our disposal, which we'll use to increase employees' salaries."

The structure of the statement is the policy.

Three moves in one paragraph. First: gradual reform of gasoline and diesel. Second: redirect the funds to a voucher system and livelihoods. Third: save on water and electricity to fund salary increases. Pezeshkian is describing a full subsidy architecture transformation — energy prices, cash transfers, and public sector pay — announced as a sequence rather than a shock.

The fuel subsidy is Iran's largest fiscal exposure. The reform is not ideological. It is arithmetic.

Iran has some of the cheapest fuel on earth. The subsidized price for gasoline is roughly 15,000 rials per litre for the first tier — a fraction of the real import-parity cost. The gap between the domestic price and the border price is the subsidy. It is one of the largest single line items in the national budget. It is also the largest single source of smuggling.

The smuggling economy is the hidden file.

The gap between Iranian subsidized fuel and neighbouring market prices is enormous. Fuel moves across the border to Pakistan, Afghanistan, Iraq, and the Gulf. The volumes are industrial. Smugglers buy at Iranian subsidized prices and sell at regional market prices. The Iranian state pays the difference. The smuggler pockets it.

The subsidy was designed as a welfare measure. It became a subsidy to the smuggling networks. The voucher system is the mechanism to end that. If the fuel price rises to near-parity, the smuggling margin collapses. The voucher replaces the subsidy for the household, not for the smuggler.

The voucher system is the redistribution layer.

The plan is not to cut support. It is to change its form. The universal fuel subsidy goes to whoever buys fuel including the smuggler, the wealthy car owner, and the border trader. The voucher goes to the registered household. The state stops paying for the smuggler's margin and starts paying the citizen directly.

That is the design. The question is the execution. The electronic voucher infrastructure the same digital payment rails that Iran has built under sanctions is the delivery mechanism. The household registers, the state credits, the voucher is spent on goods. The subsidy is preserved for the citizen and removed from the arbitrageur.

The water and electricity sentence is the other budget line.

Pezeshkian said: "If we save on water and electricity, we'll have a lot of money at our disposal, which we'll use to increase employees' salaries."

Iran's water and electricity subsidies are also massive. The price of electricity for households and industry is far below cost. The price of water is far below cost. The state pays the difference. The savings from rationalising those prices are the revenue source for the salary increase.

The water crisis in Yazd, the subsidence in the Yazd-Ardakan plain, the depletion of the aquifers those are the physical consequences of water being priced at almost nothing. If water is free, it is over-extracted. If it is priced, it is conserved. The reform is not just fiscal. It is hydrological survival.

The political risk is understood. That is why the word is "gradual."

The 2019 fuel price increase triggered nationwide protests. The state learned the lesson. A sudden price shock produces a sudden political shock. Pezeshkian is describing a phased approach: gradual reform, voucher delivery, savings redirected to salaries. The sequence is designed to keep the household whole while the price signal is introduced.

The voucher must arrive before the price rises. If the price rises and the voucher is delayed, the household feels only the loss. The sequencing is the political test. Pezeshkian is saying the sequencing will be managed.

The hidden layer: the reform is a war economy measure.

Iran is under a naval blockade. The US Navy has seized Iranian cargo ships. The sanctions architecture blocks Iranian oil exports and financial transactions. The war has cost the state billions. The budget is under pressure from every direction.

The subsidy reform is not a peacetime policy. It is a war economy measure. The state cannot afford to subsidise the smuggler. It cannot afford to subsidise the over-consumption of water and electricity while the aquifers collapse. It cannot afford to pay salaries from a budget that is bleeding.

Pezeshkian is telling the public that the reform is the condition for the salary increase. The savings from the subsidy rationalisation are the funding source. The state is not printing money to pay salaries. It is reallocating the subsidy.

The contradiction the reform answers.

For decades, the Islamic Republic subsidised fuel, water, and electricity to protect the poor. The result was that the rich, the smuggler, and the over-consumer captured most of the subsidy. The poor paid the price in smog, water scarcity, and a budget that could not fund public sector pay.

The voucher system reverses the capture. It directs the support to the registered household. The price signal goes to the market. The smuggler loses his margin. The household keeps its support.

That is the reform. It is not a neoliberal cut. It is a re-targeting of the subsidy from the arbitrageur to the citizen. The distinction matters. The Western press will call it "austerity." It is the opposite, it is the recovery of the subsidy from the networks that captured it.

The message to the employees.

Pezeshkian said the savings will go to salary increases. That is the contract. The employees accept the gradual reform, and the state delivers the pay rise. The sequencing is the guarantee. If the state delivers the voucher and the salary, the reform holds. If it does not, the 2019 memory returns.

The message to Washington.

The sanctions and the blockade were designed to force Iran into a budget crisis. Pezeshkian is answering with a structural reform that reduces the state's exposure to the smuggling economy, re-targets the subsidy to the household, and funds the public sector pay from the savings. The blockade is not producing collapse. It is producing reform.

The ledger.

The fuel subsidy goes to the voucher. The water and electricity savings go to salaries. The smuggler loses the margin. The household keeps the support. The state stabilises the budget. The sequencing is gradual. The trigger is the delivery of the voucher before the price rise.

Pezeshkian said the issues will be resolved step by step. The steps are the policy. The voucher is the mechanism. The salary is the contract. The smuggler is the loser. The household is the priority. That is the reform.
